title: Business Management SL · Set A · Paper 2

questions.title: Section A · Clayfold Studio
questions.stem: Clayfold sells refillable cups at CU 18 each. The monthly fixed costs of its workshop are CU 18,000. Variable cost is CU 8 per cup. Current monthly sales are 2,400 cups. Capacity is 3,000. A school offers to buy 500 extra cups per month at CU 13 each. These cups would also need packaging costing CU 1 each. Regular selling prices and fixed costs would stay the same.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the current monthly break-even output and margin of safety in units.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the additional monthly profit from the school order and explain one condition behind the calculation.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain one risk to Clayfold’s regular sales from accepting the discounted order.

steps.text: The selling price of a unit less its variable cost.
It is the amount available toward fixed costs and then profit.
Contribution is 18 − 8 = CU 10.
Break-even is 18,000/10 = 1,800 cups.
Margin of safety is 2,400 − 1,800 = 600 cups.
Additional unit contribution is 13 − 8 − 1 = CU 4.
Monthly gain is CU 2,000.
Combined sales of 2,900 fit within the stated capacity.
Existing sales must be retained and other costs unchanged.
Regular buyers may learn the school price.
They may negotiate discounts or postpone buying.
That would lower contribution on the larger regular sales base.

questions.title: Section A · Isla Bakery
questions.stem: Isla begins July with CU 4,600 cash. July and August receipts are CU 12,800 and CU 16,500 respectively. Ordinary cash payments are CU 15,100 and CU 14,200. An oven deposit of CU 4,000 is due in July and is additional to those payments.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct the two-month cash-flow forecast, showing net cash flow and closing balance for each month.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two ways Isla could address the July shortage, including one drawback of each.

steps.text: July outflows are 19,100, including the deposit.
July net flow is −6,300 and closing cash is −1,700.
Carry −1,700 into August and calculate net flow of 2,300.
August closes at CU 600.
Negotiate a later or staged oven deposit.
The supplier could delay installation or withdraw the price.
Arrange short-term overdraft finance covering at least CU 1,700.
Interest and bank approval may be costly or uncertain.

questions.title: Section B · Option 1 · Cedar Books
questions.stem: An independent bookshop has annual revenue of CU 200,000, cost of sales of CU 128,000 and other operating expenses of CU 54,000. Its manager proposes paid evening events. Expected event revenue is CU 24,000, with direct costs CU 11,000 and additional operating expenses CU 9,000. Daytime trade is assumed unchanged. Staff say evening transport is unreliable. A survey of 40 current members found 30 interested in talks, but only 12 willing to pay the proposed price.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the current gross profit margin.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate operating profit and operating profit margin if the proposal meets its forecasts.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two limitations of the market research for this decision.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether Cedar Books should launch regular paid evening events.

steps.text: Gross profit is CU 72,000.
Margin is 36%.
Current operating profit is CU 18,000.
Add incremental profit of CU 4,000.
Forecast operating profit is CU 22,000.
Current members omit potential new customers.
Their preferences can misstate demand from the broader market.
Interest in a talk differs from willingness to pay.
Only 12 of 40 indicated willingness, so forecasting sales from the 30 interested would overstate demand.

The forecast raises profit from 18,000 to 22,000 and the margin from 9% to 9.82%. There is little buffer if paid attendance falls short. Staff transport could raise costs or affect retention. Trial a small number of prepaid events, set a minimum booking threshold and check staffing costs before committing. Community engagement could justify a smaller direct return if daytime sales also increase. Use best fit across the response. 0 gives no creditable response. At 1–2, identify a relevant issue with little development. At 3–4, explain a point with limited case evidence. At 5–6, develop a relevant argument using case evidence. At 7–8, weigh competing arguments using specific evidence and reach a supported judgement. At 9–10, sustain a balanced case-specific judgement, explain a material limitation or condition and show how it affects the decision. Credit a different conclusion when the analysis supports it.

questions.title: Section B · Option 2 · Valewood Cycles
questions.stem: Valewood charges CU 60 per repair package. Each package uses CU 24 in parts and paid labour. Its annual fixed costs are CU 72,000 and it sells 2,500 packages. A mobile service would increase fixed costs by CU 18,000, keep the same unit costs and prices and bring in an estimated 650 additional packages. Two mechanics would alternate between the workshop and the van. Survey responses came from an online cycling club.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the extra packages needed to cover the extra fixed costs and the annual change in profit if the forecast is correct.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two non-financial factors affecting the reliability of the forecast.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Discuss whether Valewood should introduce the mobile service.

steps.text: Contribution is 2,500 × 36 = CU 90,000.
Annual profit is CU 18,000.
Extra fixed costs divided by 36.
500 extra packages.
Expected extra contribution is 650 × 36.
Expected increase is CU 5,400.
The club sample excludes casual cyclists.
Its reported interest may overstate repeat demand.
Mechanics divide their time between two locations.
Delays in the workshop could reduce existing customer retention.

The estimate exceeds the 500-package threshold by 150, but a loss of existing work or travel costs could consume the CU 5,400 gain. Customers without transport may value home repairs and generate repeat business. Test one route with paid appointments and measure workshop waiting times. Adopt if incremental volume, actual travel costs and service quality support expansion. Use best fit across the response. 0 gives no creditable response.
